questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design per-tenant controls using Kubernetes primitives and sidecar patterns.

## Key Concepts
- Per-tenant state with token bucket
- Namespace ConfigMap watch / refresh
- Sidecar deployment partnering with main gateway
- Fallback defaults and safe testing in one namespace

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf-tenantRateLimit
  namespace: cnf-system
data:
  tenants.json: |-
    {
      "tenants": {"tenantA": 100, "tenantB": 50},
      "defaultRPS": 20
    }
```

```yaml
# sidecar snippet: mount ConfigMap and read /etc/cnf/tenants.json
volumeMounts:
  - name: tenant-rates
    mountPath: /etc/cnf
volumes:
  - name: tenant-rates
    configMap:
      name: cnf-tenantRateLimit
```

```yaml
# one-namespace manifest (test-tenant)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-tenant
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gateway
  namespace: test-tenant
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gateway
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: cnf/gateway:latest
        - name: rate-limit-sidecar
          image: cnf/sidecar-rate-limit:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tenant-rates
              mountPath: /etc/cnf
      volumes:
        - name: tenant-rates
          configMap:
            name: cnf-tenantRateLimit
```

## Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Ingress] --> B[RateLimiter Sidecar]
  B --> C[Gateway Backend]
```

## Why This Is Asked
CNF reliability hinges on runtime trust alongside image provenance. This question tests practical knowledge of in-cluster attestation, trust roots, and controlled upgrades across clouds.

## Key Concepts
- Runtime attestation, KMS-backed keys, central attestation service
- Image provenance and policy enforcement against a root of trust
- Canary upgrades and per-CNF rollback in multi-namespace/multi-cloud
- Minimal in-namespace validation and rollout gating

## Code Example
```yaml
# Example policy (illustrative)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-attestation
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: attestation-check
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["CNFDeployment"]
    validate:
      message: "Attestation must be present and signed"
      pattern:
        metadata.attestationSigned: true
```

```yaml
# Attestation report (illustrative)
attestation:
  signer: "kms://arn:aws:kms:..."
  root: "root-of-trust-xyz"
  status: "valid"
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle attestation revocation and key rotation without downtime?
- What are the failure modes if the central attestation service is unavailable, and how would you mitigate them?

Tests ability to design multi-tenant observability that preserves data boundaries and privacy, a common real-world requirement in CNF platforms.

- Per-namespace (tenant) isolation

```yaml
  mode: deployment

    processors:
      batch: {}
      attributes:
        actions:
          - key: tenant_id

          endpoint: otlp-collector.central.svc.cluster.local:4317
```

## Why This Is Asked
Real-time revocation is critical when tenants share a gateway and secrets can be leaked. This task tests how to propagate revocation quickly without affecting healthy tenants, plus how to wire in-cluster trust with per-tenant isolation.

## Key Concepts
- In-cluster CA and Kubernetes CSR workflow
- Short-lived certificates and automatic rotation
- CRL generation, signing, and distribution
- Envoy/WASM-based revocation checks and sidecar reloads
- Namespace-scoped test manifests for validation

## Code Example
```javascript
// Minimal CSR manifest (YAML content as string)
const csrYaml = `
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  name: tenantA-csr
spec:
  groups:
  - system:authenticated
  request: <base64 CSR>
  usages:
  - digital signature
  - key encipherment
  - client auth
`;
```
```javascript
// CRL distribution content (as YAML string)
const crlYaml = `
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf-crl
  namespace: cnf
data:
  crl.pem: |-
    -----BEGIN X509 CRL-----
    ...
    -----END X509 CRL-----
`;
```
```javascript
// Test manifest as YAML string
const testYaml = `
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: tls-test-client
  namespace: test-tenant
spec:
  containers:
  - name: curl
    image: curlimages/curl:7.88.1
    command: ["sh","-c","curl --cacert /certs/ca.crt --cert /certs/tenantA.crt --key /certs/tenantA.key https://gateway.example.com/health"]
`;
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale CRL propagation across regions?
- What are alternatives to CRLs in high-availability environments?

## Why This Is Asked
This tests ability to implement zero-downtime upgrades in a multi-tenant CNF gateway, focusing on per-tenant isolation, cross-namespace coordination, and robust failure handling.

## Key Concepts
- Graceful drain: per-tenant drain window, preStop, readiness gates
- Global upgrade control: ConfigMap flag
- Control-plane signaling: endpoint or event
- Failure modes: stuck drains, failed signal, burst load

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf-upgrade
  namespace: tenant-a
data:
  upgradePause: "true"
```

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gateway-tenant-a
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: cnf/gateway:latest
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:9000/drain || true"]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 9000
              protocol: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the drain behavior under bursty traffic?
- How would you handle tenants with long-lived streams (WebSockets)?

## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates candidate understanding of tenant-scoped dynamic capability negotiation and caching in cloud-native environments, ensuring isolation and correctness at scale.

## Key Concepts

- Tenant-scoped capability registry (implemented as a CRD or ConfigMap)
- Per-tenant, TTL-based cache in the sidecar for performance optimization
- Highest common version selection using semantic versioning
- HTTP 406 Not Acceptable response when no compatible version exists; graceful default fallback
- Observability: Prometheus metrics, structured logging, and distributed tracing

## Code Example

```go
// Pseudocode for version negotiation
func negotiate(upstreamVersions []string, tenantID string) string {
    tenantVersions := registry.GetVersions(tenantID)
    allowed := intersect(upstreamVersions, tenantVersions)
    if len(allowed) == 0 {
        return DEFAULT_VERSION
    }
    return highestVersion(allowed)
}
```

## Implementation Highlights

- Extract X-TENANT-ID header in sidecar middleware
- Query central registry for tenant capabilities
- Compute intersection with upstream supported versions
- Select highest compatible version using semver comparison
- Store result in tenant-scoped cache with configurable TTL
- Return 406 if negotiation fails and no default is configured
- Emit histogram metrics for negotiation latency and cache hit rates
